[ASSISTANT_SAID] Some of the most common tick-borne illnesses in horses include Lyme disease, anaplasmosis, babesiosis, and equine piroplasmosis.  
[USER] The user was surprised to learn that horses could get many tick-borne illnesses.

[ASSISTANT_SAID] To protect your horse from tick-borne illnesses, you should take the following preventive measures:  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] 1. Regularly check your horse's fur and skin for ticks, especially during peak tick season.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] 2. Use a tick repellent spray made specifically for horses.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] 3. Keep your horse's environment clean and free of debris that could attract ticks.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] 4. Remove any livestock attractants from the area around your horse's environment.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] 5. Maintain a healthy immune system in your horse through proper nutrition and health care.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] 6. Have your horse checked regularly by a veterinarian to identify and treat any tick-borne illnesses early.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] By following these precautions, you can significantly reduce your horse's risk of contracting tick-borne illnesses.  
[USER] The user asked about specific times of the year when ticks are more active.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Ticks are most active during warm weather months, typically from March to November depending on location, but can be active year-round in some areas, depending on the species of ticks.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] It's a good idea to check your horse for ticks year-round to ensure their health and well-being.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] You may also want to be more vigilant during peak tick season and after your horse has been in tall grass, wooded or brushy areas, or other areas that are known to harbor ticks.  
[USER] The user is committed to checking their horse for ticks regularly.  
[USER] The user inquired about additional information regarding tick-borne illnesses in horses.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Many tick-borne illnesses can be difficult to diagnose because symptoms can vary widely and may not appear for several weeks after exposure.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Common signs of tick-borne illnesses in horses include fever, stiffness, lethargy, loss of appetite, lameness, and joint swelling.  
[ASSISTANT_SAID] Early detection is key
